content: Superior oblique palsy is a frequent cause of vertical strabismus in both adults and children. Patients with this condition may experience symptoms such as binocular vertical diplopia or may adopt a compensatory head tilt to maintain single vision. Many symptomatic patients opt for strabismus surgery, but the most effective surgical approach for treating vertical strabismus in individuals with superior oblique palsy remains uncertain. The objective of this review was to evaluate the comparative effects of different surgical treatments, as well as non-surgical interventions or observation, for vertical strabismus in patients with superior oblique palsy. The search for relevant studies included multiple databases and clinical trial registries up to December 13, 2016, without restrictions on language or publication date. The review included randomized trials that compared at least one type of surgical intervention to another surgical or non-surgical approach, or to observation. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of studies, extracted data, evaluated the risk of bias, and graded the quality of evidence. Two randomized trials were identified, involving a total of 45 children and adults. Both trials focused on surgical procedures aimed at weakening the ipsilateral inferior oblique muscle. One trial compared inferior oblique myectomy to a 10 mm recession, while the other compared inferior oblique disinsertion to anterior transposition (2 mm anterior to the temporal border of the inferior rectus insertion). Both studies were judged to have an unclear risk of bias due to incomplete reporting of methods and other methodological issues. Neither study reported data on the primary outcome of this review, which was the proportion of participants achieving postoperative surgical success, defined as hypertropia of less than 3 prism diopters (PD) in primary gaze. However, both studies provided data on the average reduction in hypertropia in primary gaze. In one trial, at 12 months postoperatively, participants who underwent inferior oblique myectomy showed a greater average reduction in hypertropia compared to those who underwent recession, although statistical comparison was not possible due to insufficient data. In the other trial, after at least six months of follow-up, participants who underwent inferior oblique disinsertion had a smaller mean reduction in primary position hypertropia compared to those who underwent anterior transposition (mean difference [MD] -5.20 PD, 95% confidence interval [CI] -7.76 to -2.64; moderate-quality evidence). Both trials also reported the average postoperative reduction in vertical deviation during adduction. One study found that participants who underwent inferior oblique myectomy had a greater reduction in hypertropia in adduction compared to those who underwent recession, but again, statistical comparison was not possible. The other trial found that participants who underwent inferior oblique disinsertion had a smaller reduction in hypertropia in contralateral gaze compared to those who underwent anterior transposition (MD -7.10 PD, 95% CI -13.85 to -0.35; moderate-quality evidence). Secondary outcomes with sufficient data for analysis included the proportion of participants with preoperative head tilt that resolved postoperatively and the proportion of participants requiring a second surgery. These outcomes were assessed in the trial comparing inferior oblique anterior transposition to disinsertion, with both outcomes favoring anterior transposition (risk ratio 7.00, 95% CI 0.40 to 121.39 for both outcomes; very low-quality evidence). None of the participants in either group developed postoperative hypotropia or reversal of the vertical deviation. However, all participants who underwent inferior oblique anterior transposition developed elevation deficiency, which was deemed clinically insignificant, whereas no participants who underwent inferior oblique disinsertion experienced this complication. Additionally, the trial comparing inferior oblique myectomy to recession reported that no participants in either group required additional strabismus surgery during the postoperative period. In conclusion, the two trials included in this review evaluated four different inferior oblique weakening procedures for the surgical treatment of superior oblique palsy. No trials were identified that compared other types of surgical procedures for this condition. Both studies enrolled a small number of participants and provided low-quality evidence due to limitations in completeness and applicability. As a result, there is no high-quality evidence to support specific recommendations for the optimal surgical treatment of superior oblique palsy. Well-designed, rigorously conducted, and thoroughly reported randomized trials are needed to determine the most effective surgical approach for managing vertical strabismus in this disorder.
